We investigate the challenge of enhancing equilibrium stability through additional learning and adaptation, beginning with a baseline equilibrium that is already in a rationalizable state. We demonstrate that by assuming learning processes produce increasingly concentrated (degenerate) distribution over time, we can establish conditions under which a equilibrium exists that is both supported by backward induction and stable. Specifically for a broad category of three-player, non-degenerate games, a backward-induction-supported equilibrium will stabilize when learning yields moderately concentrated outcomes. We also examine a specific case involving three players and payoffs that are either all distinct or only two unique options, illustrating the resulting derived stability. However, we demonstrate that strong conditions ensuring stability cannot be guaranteed in games with four of more participants. Finally, we test our theoretical findings against experimental evidence for a generic three-player game and theoretical limits for games with higher player counts.

This study examines how epidemics propagate through networks subject to dynamic changes driven by an individualistic rewiring strategy aimed at minimizing infection risks. Unlike many previous models focusing on passive evolution, this approach allows agents to proactively restructure connectivity. The resulting mathematical framework includes free boundary conditions that define distinct regions for disease presence and absence, with unique boundaries separating these zones influenced by a structural threshold parameter. Research highlights show that increasing this parameter enhances the tendency for the disease to die out; specifically, a critical threshold is identified above guaranteeing a single stable solution. Numerical simulations support these findings and illustrate the complex dynamics of the epidemic frontier.

Recent innovations in global fitting frameworks have enabled more reliable and precise extractions of Parton Distribution Functions (PDFs), with upcoming electron-ion colliders set to further refine our knowledge of nucleon and NPDF components. Within this fitting process, the theoretical side involves implementing higher-order perturbative QCD calculations and emerging phenomenological models. Furthermore, the framework must accommodate a flexible grid in variable (x, q) space and allow sufficient degrees of freedom to capture both PDF uncertainties and systematic biases. In the domain of Decision Making enhanced by Variance Reduction Experience Replay (VE-RER), it prioritizes previously selected actions within the candidate historical experience pool to bolster learned policies. Since 2019, similar approaches have gained significant attention; for more hands, these methods are valuable because they require less historical data for training. While existing works assume access to an abundant repository of past transitions, our analysis highlights a critical flaw: variance in importance sampling estimates may incorrectly amplify the probability of actions that maximize the current policy but were infrequently selected in the historical dataset based on that policy's bias. To resolve this, we propose a feedback-enhanced algorithm that utilizes the proposed update's variance estimate. Unlike the current state-of-the-art which relies on standard deviation sampling to reinforce actions with high expected reward and low uncertainty, our proposal strengthens actions with high expected reward and high uncertainty (low standard deviation sampling). This approach forces exploration into uncertain areas of the state-action space, thereby enhancing the overall policy. Extensive testing across various tasks with both On- and Off-line environments confirms that our method outperforms current state-of-the-art methods.

We introduce MultiTalk, a dataset and dynamic testing environment featuring 41,322 dialogue turns organized into 1,000 distinct top-level conversation topics. By utilizing a "think-with-us" methodology to develop extensive, highly structured dialogue trees, we created this system to overcome the limitations of existing study papers that often rely on simplistic, linear exchanges. The resulting diversity of possible user inputs and corresponding agent trajectories serves as a robust benchmark, allowing for the evaluation of dialogue strategies, performance outcomes, and technical dialogue generation capabilities. While current papers report an average of 0.3 theoretical paths per paper, our resource more than doubles this figure with over one thousand actual topics. We hope that researchers utilizing our dynamic environment can demonstrate whether their proposed innovations outperform those conducted with the original dataset, potentially yielding a tenfold improvement in conversational performance. Furthermore, the accompanying web interface offers a user-friendly platform for exploring this extensive dialogue structure.

This study explores integrating propellant assistance into the propulsion system of bipedal robots, aiming for more efficient and robust locomotion. We introduce a theoretical framework connecting ground reaction forces, center of mass (CoM) trajectories, and consumption of propellant to identify an sub-locally optimal solution via a two-point boundary value problem (TPBVP). To support this, we derive an analytical pseudoinverse model predicting point-foot contact patch locations given a specific walking mode, point-foot landing sequence, two boundary conditions (TPBVP), and control parameters (point-foot injection rate). Because the resulting non-linear two-point boundary condition problem yields multiple stable gait patterns, we employ a mixed-integer programming approach to select the most efficient option among all feasible modes. The proposed point-foot propulsion-assisted walking strategy was tested in a point-foot robot featuring two 10-N de novo propellant tanks. Results show that propellant-assisted locomotion successfully combines the robustness of swing-based ground reactions with significantly higher efficiency compared to traditional non-propellant methods.

The strategic and flexible arrangement of time slots for uplink and downlink transmissions stands as a crucial factor in optimizing the performance of fifth-generation (5G) Long-Term Evolution (LTE) systems. This scheduling approach is especially vital for dense urban and suburban areas, where typically high downlink data rates need to be achieved while simultaneously maintaining acceptable uplink performance. Designing such flexible systems introduces significant challenges, primarily due to the bilateral demand pressure and the necessity to manage resources efficiently and fairly across both domains. To effectively address these challenges, this paper introduces a generalized Game Theoretic Framework designed specifically for TDD-scheduling in LTE networks. This model incorporates dynamic variations in uplink and downlink traffic requirements, aiming to maximize downlink utility, maximize uplink utility, and ultimately determine the most beneficial configuration based on mutual gains derived from both perspectives. Fundamentally, this framework operates by first capturing and assessing the varying requirements of all user equipment (UE) within the cell, subsequently utilizing these requirements to establish a non-cooperative game. Through this game structure, it identifies a Nash Equilibrium configuration that represents an optimal balance and allocation of resources according to actual UE needs. To demonstrate the framework's efficacy, this study applies it in a practical setting as a real-time scheduler for Dynamic LTE-Scheduling (TDD), where it exhibits superior performance and adaptability compared to the conventional, static scheduling method.

Previous research predominantly relied on tuning linguistic model hyperparameters by conducting experiments on a single train/test split, utilizing a validation set drawn from that data for parameter adjustments. Elvino et al. coined the acronym CLO to emphasize the synergistic efforts between University Learning Objectives and Elvino. Current data-driven methods, however, often neglect key components when acquiring knowledge through teaching, such as the learning algorithms suitable for specific tasks, data preprocessing strategies, and the evaluation metrics most relevant to a given problem. To address these shortcomings, we conducted Educator Pupil Studies for knowledge acquisition (ELvino objectives) with Information Search Recommendation (ISS) Recommendation. In our experiment with an undergraduate student search issue, we evaluated various knowledge acquisition strategies including teacher techniques, the architecture of neural networks, the preprocessing of the knowledge, and the evaluation metrics. Our findings revealed that educators particularly influenced both the performance and ranking of knowledge transfer tasks. For instance, manipulating evaluation metrics and preprocessing strategies had a more significant impact on a search recommendation task than the architecture of the neural network itself. In summary, our results indicate that knowledge acquisition through teaching is more effective when paired with a learning architecture well-suited to the task at hand.

Findin the state satisfying the Maximum Posterior Expected (MPE) probability, or resolving large-scale constrained optimization problems, becomes unfeasible using standard graphical models when the conventional function representation requires excessive memory and processing time. In this paper, we introduce QAMD—a novel representation termed Quasi-Almost Monotone Data-Function—that replaces the traditional graph-based approach. We demonstrate theoretically that QAMD uniquely characterizes the maximum likelihood solution under specific optimization constraints. Furthermore, we define an efficient algorithm designed to identify the distinct function segments defining this maximum likelihood outcome. Empirical results indicate that compared to standard methods, utilizing QAMD drastically accelerates MPE calculations while significantly improving performance in constrained optimization tasks.

We investigate the fidelity of photon recoil effects in single-beam optical pumping spectra for the alkaliearth metal Sr, revealing a significant influence of Doppler-broadened sidebands arising due to recoil in a single laser beam. We evaluate both theoretical models and experimental data from high-fidelity vector polarization light, offering insights into optimization strategies for minimizing these phenomena. Ultimately, we conclude that careful tuning of polarization, intensity, and frequency in single-beam schemes can sufficiently mitigate photon recoil to meet high-precision requirements for tests of fundamental physics and precise clock measurements.

Disorders ranging from suspensions, granular media, and active matter exhibit abrupt transitions to sudden thickening upon slight increases in shear rate or stress. This review examines the universal principles and theoretical frameworks explaining these events, emphasizing how particle-scale mechanisms drive macroscopic behavior. We specifically address the limitations of the standard continuum mechanics approach in thickening systems and explore alternative "scaled scaling" methodologies that integrate scaling laws for stress with characteristic lengths associated with particle rearrangement. Additionally, we detail our understanding of the first three primary categories of shear-thickening behavior: first-order transitions, disorder-to-order transitions, and friction-induced transitions. By synthesizing these diverse scaled systems, this work highlights emerging patterns of global scaling and offers a unified perspective on the physics of shear-thickening phenomena.

We recall the recently defined higher rank Racah algebra $R(n)$ and introduce a new finding demonstrating that the centralizer $Z_n(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ within the $n$-fold symmetric Lie algebra $\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb{C})$ is isomorphic to the algebra $R(n)$. Furthermore, by leveraging this isomorphism, we determine the generators of $Z_n(\sl_2)(\mathbb{C})$ alongside their specific commutation relations. Finally, within a rational setting involving the quantum $\mathrm{SL}_2$ group, we identify additional generators that satisfy a similar structural framework. All considered algebras exhibit infinite polynomial centralizers; for $Z_{q-n}(\sl_2)$ in its quantum form, we derive the infinite Hilbert-Poincaré series by recognizing a functional equation satisfied by the centralizer coefficients $\omega_k^R(q,n)$ of $\omega_{q-N(n)}(\mathbb{C})$.

Google's web search personalization algorithm is hypothesized to skew a significant portion of clickable content toward greater positivity, while simultaneously suppressing unemotional and licensed material; furthermore, it may diminish around thirty percent of user attention span, effectively reducing the informational yield of typical queries, even regarding non-sensical or emotional search terms, as experimental evidence confirms, thereby demonstrating that individuals exposed to personalized settings overlook substantial information compared to those utilizing non-personalized methods.

This study outlines a conceptual design for an inject-on-the-fly (IoT) system intended to validate TeV-scale muon-ion accelerators, leveraging the Tevatron's upgraded Main Ring (mr) as a target facility. Achieving muon-ion acceleration requires ionizing atoms containing bound muons immediately prior to injection into the first ring, thereby increasing their mass-tocharge ratio and allowing the first ring to operate with optics tuned for higher-mass protons while accommodating higher-mass muonic ions. While traditional ionization methods often result in significant emittance growth due to multiple scattering during passage through thin foils, this proposed method emphasizes minimizing such scattering to preserve the beam quality necessary for later injection into subsequent rings in the accelerator complex, ultimately demonstrating the technical feasibility of this mode of pre-injection.

T2-weighted 3D MRI for abdominal imaging offers an essential tool for assessing various pathological movements, including tumor motions driven by breathing. However, signal losses and image blurring resulting from respiratory motion hinder accurate, breath-holding assessments of pathologies that move dynamically. Furthermore, these effects include increased total scan duration, a limitation that is particularly problematic for patients who cannot stay still or tolerate breath control. This work presents an interleaved, multiple single-shoot sequences combining field-cycled ultrashort repetition times (RT) with multiple free-breathing segments or views to generate T2-weighted 3D images in real time that are both rapid and robust. These sequences were evaluated using phantom studies comparing them against conventional methods, as well as in vivo tests in both healthy volunteers and patients with liver metastases, focusing on scan efficiency, robustness, and visual quality relative to standard clinical breath-hold T2 scans (specifically CSPAMM). Additionally, the proportion of k-space coverage for each free-breathing segment was evaluated, along with a quantitative analysis comparing image quality between our proposed method and the CSPAMM sequence using breath retention. This study demonstrates, through in vivo comparisons, that our new free-breathing approach delivers superior robustness against motion artifacts compared to the gold-standard breath-hold CSPAMM T2 sequence used in hospitals. Quantitative evaluation confirmed higher image quality for our method than for the breath-hold sequence, and total scan duration averaged approximately 100 seconds

A frequently encountered scenario in statistical testing involves assessing a structured test statistic that yields values within a well-defined, finite range. We approach the problem of precise p-value calculation for such statistics by formulating them as unstructured, non-negative integer sum-of-chains Markov chain (NC-MC) on a finite, discrete domain equipped with an explicit, conservative weighting scheme. Leveraging this general Markov chain framework, we construct several sophisticated testing statistics: a p-value examiner for the Paired t-test and specific p-value detectors for A/B testing scenarios involving categorical data.

This study introduces a comprehensive, longitudinal dataset for the container transport sector covering the period 1966–2013. The resource integrates historical records on industry metrics such as newbuilding costs, secondhand values, and equipment scrap prices alongside operational statistics. Specifically, it includes North American cargo volumes, U.S.-origin newboat constructions, and derived indices for capital expenditure (newbuilding and secondhand/scraper prices). Additionally, the authors present research and development indices for these cost factors based on related studies. Finally, the paper offers simple computational methods to estimate global secondhand and scrap prices utilizing limited observations of new equipment and local used or discarded assets.

Triangulation-based approaches offer a flexible framework for analyzing and reshaping surfaces, with recent innovations in "fabric spaces" offering a paradigm for integrating global and local modifications to their topological structure. These fabric spaces contrast with change-based triangulation methods, which utilize operations like edge flips, splits, and collapses to manage the evolution of triangulations. This work establishes a unified connection between the two concepts by demonstrating how to evolve a standard triangulation into a fabric space, thereby endowing the resulting configuration with inherent geometric properties.

Discretization approaches for partial differential equations often embed the original problem's physical properties as crucial elements for achieving high solution accuracy. However, the integration of these features typically introduces complexities in both analysis and computational efficiency. This paper introduces a class of Krylov subspace methods specifically designed to address such problems equipped with internal structure-defined Kryloid elements. Exploiting the embedded properties of the matrix operators, these methods offer higher efficiency compared to standard Krylov techniques, while our general framework notably encompasses standard Multigrid methods as a specialized case.

Pain resulting from the detachment of skin or underlying tissues, known as a degloving injury, poses a significant and challenging clinical issue. Skin-surface Computerized Tomography (CT) registration offers a promising approach for identifying these painful regions; however, current methodologies often yield inaccurate results when applied to real-world scenarios. Most existing techniques infer the three-dimensional structure by combining two-dimensional CT slices with biophysical assumptions, typically modeling the limb as an incompressible cylinder where internal volumes map strictly to surface features at equal distances. This study introduces a novel, data-driven biomechanical model designed specifically for skin-surface registration. Our approach integrates high-fidelity whole-limb CT segmentations of skin, muscle, fat, and bone with experimental data documenting shifts in key points before and after surgical de-gloving. Moving beyond the traditional "constant distance" assumption, we derive a surface-to-volume alignment strategy grounded in realistic biomechanical principles that incorporate shear and mass changes caused by injury. The resulting optimization framework utilizes a stiffness matrix representing tissue interactions to find the configuration that best fits all junctions within the organ systems involved in the injury. Tests on both realistic digital phantoms and an authentic clinical de-gloving injury case demonstrate that using this data-informed biomechanical framework substantially improves the accuracy of 3D-reconstructed injury scenarios compared to current standard methods.

Most methods for flow estimation in depth image pairs rely on metric learning, utilizing flow indicators like optical flow constraints to enhance performance and efficiency. Due to the inherent difficulties of simultaneously and accurately measuring both depth and motion-related changes, we propose the hypothesis that current depth-ablation approaches are vulnerable to adversarial and undettable motions and depth changes (AAUDCs). Supporting this, experimental evidence confirms the existence of an instance where real-time flow estimation algorithms produce substantial errors while also exhibiting significant optical flow violations. While the real-time flow framework remains robust regarding undetectable motions, it appears more exposed to errors; however, the framework's reliance on potentially flawed optical flow constraints allows for exploitation. We investigate the real-time flow model by analyzing its sensitivity to various parameters and demonstrate that manipulating just a single hyperparameter is sufficient to substantially increase its real-time flow errors. In today's data-driven landscape, efficiently categorizing information is crucial, yet many existing high-accuracy models fall short by being impractical for large-scale or real-time deployment due to excessive computational demands. This inefficiency is particularly evident in deploying models like Random Neural Networks (RNNs)—known to deliver top-tier performance—because their training and training procedures consume prohibitive energy and resources. This paper introduces a novel, energy-efficient algorithm that achieves top-tier classification by integrating sparsity with neural network architecture. The proposed solution delivers performance space- and time-near to that of a Bayes classifier on the fly, closely emulating the biologically plausible mechanisms of an RNN. The results suggest that deploying the offered algorithm can deliver substantial economic advantages and environmental sustainability when used in real-world applications.

Using a state equation for cold matter formed by three flavors of non-degenerate stars, we have investigated the thermal, mechanical, and magnetic characteristics of aligned configurations at various temperatures. These systems are subject to a externally applied magnetic field that influences them through a pressure-dependent critical electric field strength ranging from approximately 10 to 20 MeV. Our derived general formulas for the critical field, which accounts for spin alignment and thermal effects, facilitate numerical analysis across a broad spectrum of conditions. The associated thermal corrections induce minor fluctuations in these values. However, alignment can lead to increased central densities, maximum central magnetic/thermal fields, and a possible enhancement in the total system's maximum mass limit. Despite these internal intensifications, the overall maximum mass remains largely consistent with the well-known Landau result of ~2 GeV and the ScVDH star model of ~2.35 GeV. This study presents a preliminary framework that invites further refinement via updated state equations and a more sophisticated treatment of quantum corrections.

The strategic allocation of system resources like CPU time slices is vital for container performance and overall system stability. While heuristic-based schedulers exist, they often require extensive trial and error to function optimally. This study introduces Pause, innovative policy-learning algorithms designed to discern the impact of varying CPU allocation limits on individual microservices. Leveraging a realistic and scalable testbed known as Timeloops, Pause employs a looped policy evaluation framework to acquire valuable insights from prior configurations, significantly cutting down the learning curve for heuristic strategies such as Prognosis. Our findings indicate that implementing learned policies can boost the 94th percentile latency threshold by up to 70 percent compared to standard container default settings without compromising total throughput. Furthermore, increasing the number of learned services in the environment amplifies performance gains, highlighting the critical nature of system-wide application learning. Regarding individual applications, enhancing the accuracy of learned strategies for services with high variance in timing requirements results in a 94th percentile latency improvement of 32 percent relative to using only the baseline default limits.

The paper establishes the existence of a control function $f$ on a specific boundary segment $\Gamma_0$ of the spatial domain $\Omega$ such that both the prey and predator populations vanish completely within some finite time $T>0$ given any initial condition. The proof relies on the two-sided estimates for the dual observability inequality for the corresponding degenerate system. The result presented here extends earlier findings regarding non-degenerate prey-predator systems (as discussed in references [8, 9]). Evaluating decision-making in dynamic, high-stakes soccer situations represents a complex reinforcement learning challenge. We examine foul or free kick choices within a competitive professional league, focusing on attacks that offer an expected goal (xG) advantage exceeding a specific, neutral threshold. Our framework includes an intricate state space reflecting the kicking situation, opposing defensive arrangements, and historical xG data from analogous past instances; from this state, we derive state-action probabilities using a randomized policy. We utilize an offline approach grounded in a Markov Decision Process (RL) trained on an extensive two-season dataset spanning 36 rounds, where our model achieved precision and recall metrics of 0.40 and 0.46, respectively, in predicting top-tier model predictions. Our proposed strategy demonstrated a 4\% relative improvement in expected goals compared to the league's most successful approach. Nonetheless, in the particular sub-contexts generating these elevated predictions, our model functions with a stochastic nature. Consequently, we employ an undetermined classification for these scenario outputs. To visualize the model's distributional nature, we present the probability of executing each potential pass type along a scale from 0 to 1. Finally, we discuss certain limitations and future trajectories to refine this "randomized" strategic framework.

In exploratory drilling, the inherent low signal-to-noise ratio of seismic signals, combined with the risks of catastrophic equipment and financial loss, strongly favors avoidance of known or suspected fault zones and salt diapirs. Traditionally, geophysicists rely on high-frequency stacking-gain inversion imaging to construct velocity models and identify hazardous zones; however, this method fails to provide the high-resolution waveform information necessary for precise hazard assessment in complex settings. Conversely, waveform inversion (WI) offers exceptional detail for this purpose but is currently hindered by the necessity of iterating in the frequency domain—a process that is computationally prohibitive when applied across multiple high-frequency bands. This paper introduces a novel time-domain enhanced impedance (EI) algorithm designed to identify safe corridors with optimal parameters. The proposed approach leverages an elliptical Hamiltonian characteristic curve within the time domain to dramatically reduce both memory requirements and computational costs. Furthermore, the study validates the method through a synthetic salt dome experiment, demonstrating that the EI algorithm outperforms the standard frequency-iterative WI framework in accurately recovering Earth-impendance models, successfully highlighting the distinct geometric and physical boundaries between salt and stratigraphic layers.

This study examines the impact of an invasion by an extant species on a pair involving a displacement superiority (where a competitive advantage correlates with lower spatial ranges). Within this system, only two of these pairs naturally survive; consequently, any additional species must exclude at least one resident to reach coexistence. We analyze a one-dimensional grid-based, stochastic chaotic voting model characterized by such tradeoffs. The dynamic determines exclusion or stable existence based on whether new entrants interact with contracts that are transitive or contain cyclic exclusion cycles. We observe that in an unlimited number of scenarios with cyclic relationships, diversities grow unbounded as community diversity approaches infinity. Although this system operates under intrinsic constraints limiting total living numbers to a maximum of three above any given threshold of population density required for all members to reach a minimum level, it also demonstrates that diversity can persist across an extensive parameter range even when competition follows a strictly monotonic (transitive) hierarchy.

In an information and energy ecosystem integrating infrastructure-based and device-to-device (D2D) communication, along with renewable energy harvesting, we address the challenge of jointly optimizing power transmission, information caching, and data request routing to maximize network-wide utility. This framework accounts for inter-and intra-base station (BS) interactions, as well as dynamic changes in the demand of D2D users. To enable users to obtain information more efficiently, we propose integrating Intellect Reflecting Surfaces (IRS) into the deployment of small cell access points (SCAPs). The proposed framework models the utility function as a balance between energy consumption and network revenue, specifically incorporating a quadratic cost of data backhauling from small cells to remote servers. We formulate a mixed-integer quadratic program (MIQP) aimed at optimizing cache placement, cache allocation, energy allocation, and request scheduling within the information-energy-D2D framework. Given the difficulty of solving the MIQP directly, we develop an effective decomposition-based iterative algorithm. Numerical simulations support the problem formulation, validate the proposed solution algorithm, demonstrate the IRS technology impact, and verify results across various network conditions.

Vertical (2D) scan measurements were obtained by configuring a single-point Laser Doppler Vibrometer (LDL) into a fully scanning mode. Because acquiring these measurements requires manually navigating the target location, the project aimed to automate and simplify this process. This involved selecting an appropriate LDL system, configuring the necessary software, and developing a custom, user-friendly interface. Consequently, a system was created that allows for the rapid and efficient acquisition of comprehensive vertical scan data for any specific point, simply by clicking a 2D representation of that point within the application.

Although current developments in TEM technology show great promise, cost remains a significant hurdle; therefore, leveraging existing components for new applications is essential. This study investigates the feasibility of utilizing a programmable spatial light modulator (SLM) as a computationally controlled phase disc to replace the standard corrector plate in a TEM. We demonstrate that utilizing a programmable SLM instead of a fixed corrector allows for the dynamic control and correction of aberrations caused by sample and lens fluctuations, thereby enabling flexible 4D data collection. Comparisons of images obtained with corrections from both solutions reveal comparable spatial resolutions and contrast levels, with the added advantage of an approximately 30 percent reduction in overall system cost. We also identify that key benefits include increased experimental agility, reduced experimentalist burden, cheaper hardware, and more rapid data processing. Consequently, we argue that transitioning from static correctors to programmable phase discs represents a crucial direction for future TEM evolution.

Semantic drift occurs when a word's current meaning diverges from its past interpretations, posing a significant hurdle for natural language understanding systems. This study introduces a contextualized framework designed to detect semantic shift by integrating a bipartite structure with an adaptive input representation. For detection capabilities, the framework employs a series of discriminative tasks. Additionally, it investigates two critical challenges in standardized methodologies: the need for context-sensitive embedding for drift decisioning and the representation of gradient changes to capture semantic nuances. In our framework, these dimensions integrate to construct a unified framework for semantic shift. Evaluations using 15 decision-based datasets, along with image and text-based assessments, demonstrate that the contextualized framework, which we have designed, provides robust performance compared to state-of-theart models.

The detection of ultra-light dark matter candidates, including axions and the HDM sector (collectively known as HB), is hindered by the lack of direct observational signatures. One promising approach involves analyzing how these particles influence the rotational properties of compact astronomical bodies. A specific phenomenon occurring between certain HB dark matter candidates and neutron stars or black holes (BHOs) is known as the radiative process; the resulting prolonged emission leads to notably slower emissions. Our research provides an analytical framework for estimating the spin distributions of mass black holes resulting from radiative process, analyzing two scenarios regarding HDM composition: (i) scenarios where it represents a single self-interacting particle, and (ii) a non-interacting particulate structure like the leading candidate with different mass/charge properties. For each scenario, we identify which particulate masses permit the radiative process to occur before the related star evolves off its main sequence, deriving the predicted distribution of the related spin accordingly. These results can help constrain or predict the physical properties of the self-interacting/partitioned mass/charge properties of the most prominent particulate structure. One overarching result indicates that core rotational constraint provides the strongest evidence for heavy, low-intercept dark sectors containing self-interaction/partitioned mass/charge properties of the most prominent particulate structure.

Interkinetic nuclear movement involves the migratory motion of nuclei along the apical-basal axis during early neural development, a process critical to neuronal proliferation across vertebrates. We address the challenge of steering a population of autonomous agents with individually learned policies that possess their own behavioral tendencies toward cooperative goal attainment. Our focus centers on a newly introduced setting, dubbed "VectorD&D," which adapts Dungeons and Dragons (D&D) for the realm of theoretical and empirical analysis within a fully agent-governed environment. Equipping agents with high-capacity cooperative strategies in such settings is inherently difficult due to the inherent complexity of the D&D environment, the need to anticipate and accommodate the predictions of other agents, and the significant difficulty associated with communicating nuanced and varied intents effectively. To overcome these barriers, we establish a theoretical framework grounded in Intention Representations (IRs) and the collective execution of individual state-dependent strategies. This structure enables the application of efficient theories-of-mind (ToM) and robust reinforcement learning algorithms. Empirical results demonstrate that agents guided by the proposed representation and a standard RL baseline successfully develop a functional, high-capacity collaborative dynamic under the direction of a singular leader. Furthermore, we observe that varying the leader's reinforcement signal profoundly shapes their evolved styling and predictive capabilities over time. From a broader perspective, VectorD&D serves as a strong platform for investigating complex cooperation among autonomous systems, while our proposed framework of Intention Representations offers a versatile toolset for facilitating cooperation among predictive agents in other demanding collaborative contexts.

This study examines the dynamical behavior of nanoscale colloidal assemblies governed by strong, short-range repulsive forces, focusing on how different interaction motifs influence self-assembly. While pairwise interactions yield well-known phases like triangles and hexagons, the formation of stable triangles requires repulsive components of sufficient angular specificity. Once these triads establish, the system adopts a self-reverse phase: particles rotate within their triangular cages without disrupting the overall lattice. We provide an analytical framework grounded in effective potentials to account for this confinement motion and explore the role of non-equilibrium phase transitions. Furthermore, when triangular bonds coexist with other pairs (e.g., in quadruplets), the collective behavior shifts from the self-reverse phase to crystallization or vapor phases, driven by competing interaction forces that disrupt the symmetry needed for self-reverse ordering.

Recent observations from Parker Solar Probe indicate that energy flow in inner heliospheric regions is predominantly directed radially outward, with only about 10% moving laterally, a pattern that aligns with theoretical expectations. This study applies novel spatial mapping techniques and statistical analysis to inner heliosphere data obtained during Parker Solar Probe's first two missions to establish rigorous constraints on heliospheric energy dynamics. The findings reveal that while radial breeze energy dominates the inner heliosphere, non-negligible lateral components persist; specifically, up to approximately 20% of total breeze energy can flow transversely toward the heliospheric current sheet (HSX). Such ratios fluctuate based on location relative to the HSX, orientation of the radial magnetic field, and plasma parameters such as the plasma beta. These observations provide critical validation for gradient diffusion and turbulent remnant theories, highlighting the necessity of advanced statistical frameworks to accurately assess heliospheric energy dynamics.

Spatial capture-recapture (SCR) has emerged as a vital tool for estimating animal population densities and individual characteristics when physical capture indicators, like unique tags or genetic profiles, are available. Dark Matter (DM) halos, along with their resident galaxies, exhibit a range of structural and dynamical characteristics that are intrinsically linked through various physical processes. While the standard $\Lambda$CDM cosmological model predicts that the properties resulting from accretion and merger histories should primarily define dark matter halos—specifically through halo formation time—validating this scenario remains challenging due to the difficulty in reconstructing halo history observationally. Consequently, researchers often employ the central galaxies' properties within halos as proxies to infer dark matter dynamics and testing fields. Nevertheless, emerging evidence from both simulations and observations hints that the velocity distribution of dark matter itself constitutes a distinct class of observable data capable of independently constraining cosmological models, potentially offering a more robust solution than relying solely on central galaxy attributes.

Inspired by these findings, we applied deep learning techniques to investigate whether the velocity dispersion within dark matter distributions can serve as an independent predictor for the mass of dark matter clusters, complementing the traditional use of stellar mass and formation time. Our analysis reveals that inclusion of velocity dispersion significantly enhances the accuracy of dark matter cluster regression tasks compared to models utilizing only formation time and stellar mass specifically demonstrating that a deep neural network (DNN) architecture outperformed traditional Machine Uniform Ensemble Regression (MUSER) methods in these scenarios.

Assuming massive protostars grow via a accretion process despite forces that typically drive stellar winds and limit such force, represents a long-standing enigma in our field. Recent observations from the Submillimeter Array reveal that massive young stellar objects emit strong, periodic shocks caused by a disk undergoing periodic contraction and expansion, suggesting periodic infall may help explain how high-mass stars form. Using advanced three-dimensional radiation-hydrodynamics modeling, our study reveals two key phenomena: (1) as an object approaches higher masses, a single episodic accretion surge can merge with another, significantly exceeding the mass threshold that previously caused a similar event; (2) these massive, early-system accretion bursts are capable of producing the strong, periodic shocks that mimic those seen in high-mass young stellar systems observed from Earth today. Therefore, our research offers fresh perspectives and supporting evidence for the hypothesis that a complex interplay between hydrodynamic forces and gravity, specifically a single, massive, and multi-episodic accretion outburst, is the mechanism behind high-mass star formation.

Conditional Generative Adversarial Networks (CGANs) represent a powerful Bayesian framework for computing full conditional distributions, with applications spanning natural language processing and computer vision. Although Monte Carlo simulations have historically been the preferred method for Bayesian inference in images—often citing the high cost of sampling conditional likelihoods across numerous z samples—this study demonstrates, through extensive experiments with both synthetic and real images, that regularized conditional GANs outperform image-based Monte Carlo approaches. Specifically, we investigate Epanechnikov boundary-corrected linear samplers (ECGLS), proving via additional trials with authentic data that they often surpass image-scored variants. These findings are significant for practical Bayesian applications, particularly in remote sensing, astronomy, and chemical analysis, where collecting additional likelihood evaluations is frequently unfeasible. Consequently, the demonstrated efficacy of ECGLS ensures robust distributional sampling without excessive additional costs.

Auditory localization involves determining whether a specific sound source exists within a defined area, an ability that is critically important for applications like robotic exploration and autonomous driving. This paper introduces a new method for localizing sounds by applying point cloud literature techniques to 3D audio spatialization. Illness-aware image modification (IW) aims to transform authentic scene images into ill scene images while preserving semantic attributes of the specific disease. The problem of illness-aware image modification (IIW) has not been previously discussed, likely because of the difficulty in obtaining sufficient numbers of pathological scene images. However, an important source of data lies within real clinical scene images themselves, which typically contain pathological elements even though they are not always severe enough to qualify as true pathological images. Leveraging generative adversarial networks (GAN), we present a new framework called illness-aware modification (I2M) that maps pathological awareness from pathological images onto healthy images to produce synthetic pathological images. The source of our data comes from 1,500 pathological images and 1,500 healthy images. To test our framework's effectiveness, we conducted extensive experiments using only one hundred trained images per class (pathological and healthy) during model training. Our approach was validated through five separate tests: visual inspection, quantitative analysis, a study on class-specific awareness, and a clinical expert assessment.

ViDaExpert serves as a specialized utility for rendering and analyzing multidimensional vector datasets non-linearly. Designed intuitively for user-friendly interaction, the application is particularly effective for working with high-level semantic vector representations emerging from contemporary machine learning models such as those used for Large Language Models (LLMs). This tool establishes a sturdy bridge between these statistical vector representations and human interpreability, facilitating the creation of "navigate displays"—an innovative class of visualization where data is displayed with standard linear orthogonality while users explore via non-linear curves to capture complex data structures. Using ViDaExpert, both professionals and laypersons can seamlessly transform raw vectorized output into engaging and informative displays. This tool will prove invaluable to anyone handling or seeking to communicate machine-generated learned representations.
